content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has established a comprehensive system for the dissemination of its publications and guidelines. These materials are distributed to various entities, including WHO depository libraries, representatives, liaison officers, headquarters, regional offices, and off-site office libraries. Additionally, non-mandatory recipients such as national authorities in sexual and reproductive health, cancer control programs, national research centers, and WHO collaborating centers also receive these resources. WHO staff at all levels, relevant non-governmental organizations (NGOs), medical societies focused on cancer control or sexual and reproductive health, and scientific journals (both general and specialized) are also included in the distribution network. The WHO library database, accessible online, serves as a repository for these materials. International organizations, donors, potential publishers of translated versions, and contributors to the documents are encouraged to utilize these resources. Invitations to conferences for discussing and presenting the guidelines are welcomed, and regional conferences have already been held in the Americas and Africa in 2013 to introduce the new recommendations to stakeholders involved in national program planning. Other regions are scheduled for coverage in 2014. If requested by regional offices, WHO will support countries in adapting the guidelines to their specific needs and integrating them with existing national guidelines. This adaptation process will involve organizing workshops at regional, sub-regional, and country levels to discuss and tailor each recommendation to the national epidemiological, cultural, and socioeconomic context. Initially, the guidelines will be available in English, with translations into other languages dependent on funding availability. Efforts will also be made to encourage third-party translations into non-UN languages for broader accessibility. The evaluation of the guidelines will include monitoring the number of downloads from WHO websites as an indicator of interest. WHO regional offices will track requests from countries for technical assistance in implementing the guidelines. National stakeholder meetings will be organized to gather feedback on the clarity, feasibility, and usefulness of the recommendations. Additionally, WHO will monitor how many countries revise their national guidelines for the treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 2–3 and adenocarcinoma in situ based on the new recommendations. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) will continue to collaborate with WHO on an ad hoc basis to address research gaps identified during the guideline development process. Since the evidence search was conducted in early 2012, ongoing monitoring of the literature will be performed to identify new evidence and treatment methods. Updates to the recommendations will be considered as new evidence becomes available, with a major update anticipated approximately three years after the initial publication. The guidelines for the treatment of CIN 2–3 and adenocarcinoma in situ are supported by extensive references to studies and evidence reviews. These include research on predictors of persistent cytologic abnormalities, treatment modalities, and outcomes of various procedures such as cryotherapy, loop electrosurgical excision, and cold knife conization. The guidelines also address the safety, acceptability, and feasibility of single-visit approaches to cervical cancer prevention in low-resource settings. Declarations of interest from experts involved in the guideline development process have been disclosed. These include financial and non-financial relationships with organizations and companies involved in cervical cancer research, prevention, and treatment. For example, some experts have received funding or support for research projects, advisory roles, or speaking engagements from pharmaceutical companies and non-profit organizations.
